name: George Whitesides
stance: A leading House voice on superintelligence risk — monitoring recursive self-improvement, pausing frontier training, and catastrophic-risk red lines.

statements.text: As a member of the Armed Services Committee, I’m deeply concerned that Secretary Pete Hegseth is pressuring Anthropic to get rid of safeguards that prevent surveillance of Americans and maintain human oversight of AI-enabled weapons.
Demanded accountability from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over reports that the Pentagon pressured Anthropic to roll back its safety guardrails.
Wrote to Secretary Hegseth about his decision to terminate the Defense Department's contract with Anthropic.
Pressed the Defense Department on its public dispute involving Anthropic and OpenAI, calling for the right guardrails.
Helped secure an NDAA amendment to ensure decisions involving nuclear weapons remain in human hands, not AI.
Introduced legislation treating attempts to steal cutting-edge AI models as a danger to national defense and letting AI companies share information to reduce AI security risks.
Introduced the Self-Improving AI Monitoring Act with Rep. Harrigan, directing CAISI to monitor frontier models' autonomous AI-R&D capabilities and recursive self-improvement.
When you take humans out of the driver's seat and let machines train machines, small glitches can snowball into major security risks fast.
Joined Reps. Sam Liccardo, Ted Lieu and Lori Trahan in calling on Speaker Johnson to bring the House back into session and advance AI safeguards.
Called on Congress to remain in session through September to address the rapid advancement of AI.
I’m proposing a one-month global AI safety stand-down. AI is moving faster than our ability to understand and regulate it.
In a Washington Post op-ed, called for an industry-wide 30-day Safety Stand-Down on frontier AI development, backed by legislation.
The people building this technology put the odds of catastrophe somewhere between 1 in 100 and a coin flip.
Called on Congress to stay in Washington and work on AI safety, bringing companies, experts and government together on rules of the road.
I’m calling for a 30-day safety stand-down at the leading AI labs to establish clear red lines and meaningful safeguards before they keep pushing forward.
Pressed OpenAI, Hugging Face and Anthropic on the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident, including unexplained shutdowns and erased forensics.

AI agents went rogue. The companies that built them don’t fully understand how it happened, why it happened, or how to make sure it doesn’t happen again. That’s why I’m calling for a 30-day slowdown of AI development so we can understand the risks and draw clear safety red lines.
Speaker Johnson just canceled tomorrow’s legislative session, sending Congress home for a 7-week recess. That means no opportunity to pass AI guardrails
Instead of spending time lowering costs, passing AI safety policy, or ending the failed Iran War, Speaker Johnson sent us on vacation.
We can take the lessons learned in the aerospace industry and apply those to frontier AI.
Said AI safety cannot be left entirely to the companies building the technology and that government and industry must set guardrails together.
We’re seeing new risks emerge, and even the companies building these systems don’t fully understand everything they’re capable of.
While we discuss how to tackle AI superintelligence, we also have to address how it’s changing the way our kids learn, how we work, and how we interact with technology.
